ENT CLINICAL NOTE

Subjective:
- Presenting complaint and trigger/exposure:
  • 3-day history of “bad diarrhoea.”  
  • No recent travel, unusual food, or known infectious exposure reported.
- Symptom timeline and progression:
  • Onset 3 days ago; 4–5 loose-to-watery bowel motions/day.  
  • Mild lower abdominal pain; one episode of vomiting; possible low-grade fever.  
  • Mild ↓ appetite; able to maintain oral fluids.
- ENT symptoms:
  • Throat swelling/closure sensation: none reported.  
  • Voice change/hoarseness: none.  
  • Dysphagia/odynophagia, drooling: none.  
  • Nasal/ocular symptoms: none.  
  • Stridor/noisy breathing or dyspnea: none.  
  • Swelling (lips/tongue/uvula/face): none.  
  • Ear pain/hearing changes: none.  
  • Neck pain/swelling: none.
- Relevant past episodes and treatments:
  • Occasional similar diarrhoea after certain foods/travel in the past; self-limited.  
  • No prior hospitalisation, investigations, or injection therapy.
- Allergies and current medications:
  • Drug/food allergies: none known.  
  • Medications: inhaler described as “Lexapro,” yellow colour (dose/route/frequency not documented); no antidiarrhoeals or analgesics taken.
- Social context:
  • Location secure for consultation; no additional supervision mentioned.

Objective:
- Observable swelling: none stated.
- Airway/breathing: normal appearance per clinician; no respiratory distress.
- Mental status: normal; conversant.
- Vitals and physical examination: Not recorded.
- Accompaniment: not stated.

Assessment:
- Working clinical impression: Acute self-limited gastroenteritis (most likely viral).
  Evidence: sudden onset, watery stools 4–5×/day, single vomit, mild fever, no blood/mucus, maintained hydration.
- Differential diagnosis (aligned with DDx):
  1. Acute viral gastroenteritis – high likelihood; classic time-course and symptom pattern.
  2. Acute bacterial food-borne gastroenteritis – medium likelihood; similar presentation though no clear food/travel trigger.
  3. Medication-induced diarrhoea (if inhaler truly escitalopram/“Lexapro”) – low-medium likelihood; timing less suggestive.
  (No ENT-specific pathology suspected; airway secure.)

Plan:
- Immediate / current management:
  • Encourage adequate oral hydration; start oral rehydration salts (Dioralyte).  
  • Advise soft, easily digested diet: crackers, toast, mashed vegetables; avoid dairy, meat, fish, and eggs until symptom-free ≥ 48 h.  
- Escalation criteria / red flags:
  • Seek medical care if stool frequency ≥ 6–8×/day, signs of dehydration, blood or mucus in stool, persistent vomiting, fever, or symptoms > 7 days.
- Follow-up:
  • Stool sample and possible antibiotics if blood present or diarrhoea persists beyond one week.  
  • Re-consult/ED review if deterioration.  
  • No specific ENT or allergy referral indicated at this time.

Quality checks:
● Missing but clinically expected elements for acute ENT/allergy presentation: full vital signs (BP, HR, RR, SpO₂, Temp); focused ENT/airway exam findings; medication name/dose confirmation (unclear inhaler); explicit auto-injector availability (not applicable but typically queried).  
● Conflicts between transcript and DDx: none noted.  
● Transcript quality: clear audio; minimal inaudible segments not affecting key data.
